item.title: What you don't see
item.description:
Decades ago, I took a test in a statistics class that included a version of the classic Monty Hall problem. You might know it: a game show host presents three doors. Behind two are goats, and behind one is a car. You pick a door, the host knowingly opens one of the other doors to reveal a goat, and you’re asked whether it makes sense to switch.

But as I remember it, my exam had one important difference. It said the host opened a door randomly, rather than deliberately choosing one with a goat. I interpreted that to mean the host might accidentally reveal the car. I thought my teacher was being tricky, intentionally giving us a variation on the classic problem. I worked through the possibilities and concluded that if the host opened a door randomly, and happened to reveal a goat, switching would give you a 1 in 2 chance of winning, rather than the traditional 2 in 3.

When I got my test back the following week, I’d received a zero on that question. My teacher had simply marked the correct answer as 2 in 3. I asked whether the addition of the word “randomly” changed how we should interpret the information revealed by the host. They said no.

The question nagged at me. I’d never been particularly focused on grades. I wanted to pass my classes, but between working and participating in speech and debate, I often didn’t even turn in my homework. This was different, though. What bothered me wasn’t the grade. It was that I didn’t understand why I was wrong.

So I went home and tackled the problem the way I knew how. I wrote a small simulation, what I’d now call a Monte Carlo simulation. First, I coded the traditional version of the problem and confirmed that switching won 2 out of 3 times. Then I wrote a version where the host didn’t know where the car was and randomly opened one of the remaining doors. I discarded the games where the host accidentally revealed the car, keeping only those where he’d revealed a goat.

To my surprise, switching now won half the time.

I double-checked my code and looked again at the wording of the question. I wasn’t wrong, at least if my assumptions were correct. It felt like one of those apocryphal stories I used to hear on AM radio as a kid, where a brilliant child disagrees with their knowledgeable teacher, and that child turns out to be Albert Einstein.

I was excited to show my teacher the results. I’m not sure what I expected. I just thought they’d find what I’d discovered as interesting as I did.

That’s not the reaction I got. My teacher had no interest in the simulation and simply repeated that the answer was 2 in 3.

Looking back, I still think it’s entirely possible I was wrong. There may have been something else in the wording of the problem that I’d missed. It seems unlikely that a statistics teacher would misunderstand something like this. Or maybe they did. Even the best of us have bad days.

But the important part of the story, at least for me, was never whether I was right or wrong. It stuck with me because it was the day I fell in love with statistics and simulation. I loved the idea that you could reason your way to an answer from first principles, then check yourself by encoding your assumptions in a simulation and watching it all play out.

When I think of statistics, I naturally think of play. And that’s what I want to share with you.

Probability by counting

I grew up in a family of casual gamblers, and I’ve always loved dice games. In kindergarten, I once filled out one of those “what I like to do” assignments by drawing a picture of myself throwing dice, with “CRAPS” written in big letters above it. I remember my mom being embarrassed, not because I was playing craps, but because she worried the teacher would think I was swearing.

If you’ve played much craps, you probably already know the probability of rolling a seven. But if you don’t, it’s surprisingly easy to figure out.

We count the outcomes we want and divide by all possible outcomes. This works when the outcomes are equally likely, as they are with two fair dice.

Let’s start by listing all the possible combinations:

1,1  1,2  1,3  1,4  1,5  1,6
2,1  2,2  2,3  2,4  2,5  2,6
3,1  3,2  3,3  3,4  3,5  3,6
4,1  4,2  4,3  4,4  4,5  4,6
5,1  5,2  5,3  5,4  5,5  5,6
6,1  6,2  6,3  6,4  6,5  6,6

That’s 6 × 6 = 36 possibilities. Of those, six add up to 7:

1,6  6,1  2,5  5,2  3,4  4,3

That gives us 6/36, or 1/6 (about 16.7%), for the probability of rolling a seven.

That’s it. You’re now calculating probabilities. The arithmetic won’t get much harder than this. The tricky part is figuring out what to count, and what assumptions we’re making when we count it.

Flipping coins

Let’s say you flip a coin twice. If I tell you the first flip was heads, what’s the chance the second flip was also heads? Some gamblers will say “the coin is hot,” but as long as the flips are fair and independent, the answer is 50%. Knowing the result of one flip doesn’t change the probability of the next.

But what if, instead, we look only at pairs of flips where at least one was heads? What’s the probability that both were heads?

Now the answer is 1/3. How can that be?

Consider the four equally likely outcomes:

HH, HT,
TH, TT

By looking only at pairs where at least one flip was heads, we’ve eliminated TT. That leaves HH, HT, and TH.

When I told you the first flip was heads, only HH and HT were possible. But “at least one” also includes TH. Now we have three equally likely outcomes, only one of which has two heads.

This illustrates something important about statistics, and about how we understand the world. Even when two events are independent, we can create statistical relationships between them simply by changing which outcomes we choose to look at.

How we select our data, and how that data comes to us, matters.

Tuesday Boy Problem

Now let’s apply this to the Tuesday Boy Problem, starting with a familiar variation:

Mr. Smith has two children. The older child is a boy. What is the probability that both children are boys?

We’ll assume that each child has an equal chance of being a boy or a girl, and that the sex of one child is independent of the other.

As with the coin flips, knowing the older child is a boy tells us nothing about the younger child. The answer is 50%.

Now let’s make a small adjustment to the problem’s framing:

Mr. Smith has two children. At least one child is a boy. What is the probability that both children are boys?

Again, there are four equally likely possibilities:

BB, BG,
GB, GG

Knowing at least one child is a boy eliminates GG. That leaves three equally likely possibilities, only one of which has two boys. So the answer is 1/3.

Now for the classic version, where we also specify that the boy was born on Tuesday:

Mr. Smith has two children. At least one child is a boy born on Tuesday. What is the probability that both children are boys?

This tiny change alters how we count the possibilities. If we consider all families with at least one Tuesday-born boy, the probability shifts from 1/3 to 13/27, or about 48%.

What’s special about Tuesday? Nothing. We could say Monday, or a boy born in December.

Let’s assume birthdays are equally likely to fall on any day of the week, independently for each child and independently of their sex. We now have 7 days × 2 sexes = 14 possibilities per child. For two children, that’s 14 × 14 = 196 equally likely combinations.

Let’s count how many of those combinations have at least one boy born on Tuesday.

If the older child is a Tuesday-born boy, the younger child has 14 possibilities. If the younger child is a Tuesday-born boy, that’s another 14. But we’ve counted the case where both children are Tuesday-born boys twice, so we subtract one.

That leaves 14 + 14 − 1 = 27 possibilities.

Now, how many of those have two boys? If the older child is a Tuesday-born boy, the younger could be a boy born on any of the seven days of the week. The same goes if the younger child is the Tuesday-born boy. Again, we subtract the one case counted twice.

That’s 7 + 7 − 1 = 13 possibilities with two boys, out of 27 total. So the answer is 13/27, or about 48%.

The intuition is that families with two boys have two chances to produce a Tuesday-born boy, while families with only one boy have just one. When we filter for families with at least one Tuesday-born boy, we end up including proportionally more two-boy families.

Now, here’s an exercise for you.

Suppose instead that we meet a father, randomly select one of his two children, and ask him to describe that child. He tells us it’s a boy born on Tuesday.

What’s the probability that both his children are boys?

Think through why before revealing the answer below.

Answer

50%, for the same reason that knowing the older child is a boy born on Tuesday gives us a 50% chance that both children are boys. We’ve learned something about one randomly selected child, but nothing that changes the probability for the other child.

The difference between this and the 13/27 answer isn’t simply the words “at least one.” It’s how we obtained the information. When we select families based on whether either child meets a condition, we’re selecting from a different population than when we randomly choose one child and learn something about that child.

Same observation, different selection process, different probability.

Berkson’s Paradox

Thinking about these questions as brain teasers is, to me, the least interesting way to approach them. They become tricks you memorize rather than ideas that change how you think. These aren’t riddles. They’re ways of thinking about the information you receive, questioning where it came from, and making better decisions as a result.

And you’ve probably encountered this same phenomenon throughout your life without realizing it.

The Tuesday Boy Problem is an example of a broader phenomenon called Berkson’s paradox. The children’s sexes were independent to begin with, but selecting families based on whether either child meets a condition creates a statistical relationship between them within the group we’re looking at. More generally, two things can be completely unrelated, but if they both influence what makes it into a group, they can suddenly appear related.

Think about restaurants in touristy areas. Times Square, or right next to the Eiffel Tower. When you see a restaurant in one of those locations, do you think, “Wow, they probably have great food there!”?

Probably not. But why? Does the Eiffel Tower give off some weird odor that spoils the food?

There’s no inherent reason that a restaurant with a great location should have worse food. But imagine that, for a restaurant to survive, it needs either a great location or great food.

If a restaurant has a bad location and bad food, why would anyone go there? It will go out of business. A restaurant in a bad location needs good food to survive. A restaurant in a great location, on the other hand, can survive even if its food is mediocre.

Now, that’s not to say location and food quality have nothing to do with each other in the real world. But even if they were completely unrelated to begin with, we’d still find a negative correlation among the restaurants that survived.

The restaurants that didn’t survive are missing from our data. And because we’ve excluded them, good locations and good food appear to be negatively related, even though neither causes the other.

What we don’t see can change what we think we know about what we do see.

Is it true?

We live in a world where we have access to more information than ever before. And we’ve become increasingly concerned with whether that information is true. That’s a good thing. Truth matters.

But truth isn’t enough.

Imagine I show you twenty completely true stories about violent crimes committed around the world in the past week. What have you learned about whether crime is increasing or decreasing?

Almost nothing. You don’t know how many crimes occurred this week compared with the same period last year, or how I chose which twenty stories to show you.

Newspapers have always had editors deciding which stories were newsworthy. Those decisions were influenced by what they thought was important, what would interest their readers, and, consciously or not, their own beliefs about the world.

I had a conversation about this recently. A visitor from out of town was reading our local newspaper and remarked, “Wow, you have a lot more traffic accidents here than back home in Los Angeles.”

Maybe we do. But we’re a largely rural area, while Los Angeles has far more news competing for attention. An accident that makes the news here might not even warrant a mention there. We can’t tell how common accidents are in either place just by counting the stories in the newspaper.

Today, we have another layer. People create content they think will get attention, and algorithms select what to show us based on what we’re likely to engage with. Nobody has to lie. Nobody even has to be deliberately misleading. But the things most likely to get our attention aren’t necessarily representative of the world.

You can be told nothing but the truth and still be misled.

Monty Falls

Let’s return to the Monty Hall problem. In the classic version, the host knows where the car is and deliberately opens a door with a goat. Because the host always reveals a goat, you have a 2 in 3 chance of winning the car if you switch.

But the version of the problem on my test, or at least how I interpreted it, said the host opened a door randomly. The host might have revealed the car, but we’re only looking at the games where he didn’t.

Imagine playing 300 games. In roughly 100 of them, you initially pick the car, so the host is guaranteed to reveal a goat. In the other 200, you pick a goat, and the host has a 50% chance of accidentally revealing the car. That eliminates about 100 games, leaving us with roughly 100 games where you initially picked the car and 100 where you picked a goat. Among the games where the host revealed a goat, switching and staying are now equally likely to win.

What I love about this problem is that, from the perspective of someone watching a single game, the host has simply opened a door and revealed a goat. We observe exactly the same thing in both versions. But that observation doesn’t carry the same information when the process that produced it is different. It’s not just what we see that matters, but how it came to be.

I enjoy Bayes’ theorem as much as the next guy, but sometimes I think formulas can make relatively simple ideas seem more mysterious than they are. The difficult part isn’t always calculating the answer. It’s figuring out what question we’re actually answering, and what assumptions we’re making along the way. What are we actually looking at? How was that information generated? And perhaps most importantly, what aren’t we seeing?

An observation can be perfectly accurate and still be misleading. A correlation can be perfectly real and still tell us very little about what caused it.

Long ago, a tiny change in the wording of a test question made me question something I thought I understood. And I think that’s still what I love most about statistics.

We don’t have to choose between believing everything and doubting everything. We can learn to ask better questions. Where did our information come from? What might we be missing? Do the conclusions we’re drawing actually follow?

The goal isn’t to question everything for the sake of questioning it. It’s to understand the world a little better.

item.title: Teaching real lessons with fake worlds
item.description:
I build little worlds full of adventurers, potions, and dragons. Students run potion shops where they manage magical supply chains for demanding fighters and wizards. They run media companies providing entertainment to dragons, frog-folk, and discerning gnomes. And in the process, they become curious about how the worlds themselves work and come alive.

I worked in tech for a long time, most of it leading technical teams. I kept noticing the same thing: new grads who struggled with problems that looked nothing like their coursework. They knew how to do the work, but only if it was carefully packaged for them. In the wild, solving a technical problem is a cycle:

  1. Formulate: Translate an unbounded, ambiguous situation into a technical problem.
  2. Solve: Execute the technical solution.
  3. Interpret: Evaluate whether your solution actually solved the problem.

Even when toy problems attempt steps 1 and 3, it’s often thin pseudocontext. There isn’t enough noise, and it’s painfully obvious what technical thing needs to be done.

Large language models have made this gap impossible to ignore. Step 2—doing the technical work—is now too often solvable with a prompt→copy→paste. It’s the same shift calculators brought to arithmetic: the execution is automated, but the framing of the problem is not. Simulations let me push students into Steps 1 and 3, where intellectual work continues to thrive.

I’ve incorporated simulations into my upper-division computer science courses to teach the metacognitive and epistemic skills necessary to solve difficult problems as they actually exist.

Why Simulation?

I’ve always loved simulation-style games. Ever since playing the gold-cartridge Legend of Zelda on the NES, I’ve been fascinated by the idea that the little characters in those worlds might have lives of their own; that they might keep moving even when the player isn’t looking.

That notion is the seed of my classroom simulations: worlds that run on their own, where students must reason about living systems rather than static puzzles.

My first classroom simulation-game came out of a databases course. Early on, I realized students weren’t really feeling what it meant to run a production system: the pressure, the messiness, the human factors. Software without customers is sterile. But software that serves a live world, with people depending on it, becomes something else entirely—unpredictable, alive, and worth thinking about.

For example:

  • Teaching concurrency errors: As “customers” fire off parallel cart checkouts, students’ code runs into fun and unpredictable race conditions. Sorry, your inventory is out of sync. You had a lost update. The week after, when I lecture on transactions, you’re excited to see it solves your problem.
  • Teaching design principles: Let students debug the chaos of a mutable, update-in-place system, then guide them toward architectural patterns that reduce that pain—immutability, append-only logs, systems designed for observability. That’s how many experienced developers come to care about those principles: not from theory, but from scars.

This matters even more when teaching data science. In my Knowledge Discovery class, students build recommendation engines, churn detectors, and user personas. Simulations are foundational here because of the counterfactual: for a recommender, how do you know if it’s any good without knowing what would have happened if the user was shown different content? Offline evaluation metrics often fail to capture what only reveals itself in a live test. A simulation is a way I can bring that necessary complexity into the classroom.

Simulations also provide an ethical sandbox—an advantage over even the real world. If you deploy a recommendation engine that accidentally optimizes for outrage or suppresses a demographic, people get hurt. In my classroom, if a student’s algorithm radicalizes the gnomes or creates dystopian inequality among the frog-folk, we can pause and examine what went wrong. Consequences made visible, without the lasting damage.

How I Build Simulations

My goal when designing a simulation is for it to mimic the authentic data in the ways that matter. It has to feel genuine, even when the subject matter of the simulation is fantastical. Synthetic data too often looks fake.

There are three ways fake data tends to give itself away:

  • Correlation: Data should be a web of interesting, interconnected correlations of varying degrees.

  • Shape: Data should have the right shape for its process.

  • Time: Data should both change over time and operate cyclically; it’s influenced by the sun, the moon, and the social patterns of human life.

Correlation

Did you know that ice cream consumption and violent crime rates are frequently correlated? I asked my students this question, and one response was, “Well obviously! Crime is hard work and you need to treat yourself afterwards.” Moving on.

Why are they correlated though? We’ve all heard the phrase correlation does not imply causation. When we say that, we mostly mean direct causation. If we accept that our highly correlated world results from a web of causes—“this causes this, which causes these two things, and then those in turn cause others”—we can use that fact as the foundation for natural-looking correlations.

I draw upon Judea Pearl’s causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to make this happen. I start by drawing out a causal graph, giving each effect multiple causes, often layers and layers deep.

For example, in the interaction below, we can see how the ice-cream/violent crime correlation could arise via confounding, as illustrated using a DAG. In this case, both ice-cream consumption and violent crime depend on season (the confounder). The scatter plots show how ice-cream consumption and violent crime become correlated as a result, even without any direct causal link.

This is unrealistically transparent, though, if we actually let students see all of this. It is like the blind men and the elephant from the Tittha Sutta. One blind man feels the trunk and says “It’s a snake!” Another feels a leg and says “It’s a tree!” Yet another feels the tusk and says “No, you fools, it’s a giant spear!” Each has only a partial view of the underlying truth.

I build my “elephant” by creating a large causal DAG that naturally produces realistic correlations, but I only expose a small selection of mostly terminal nodes, and often in opaque and subtle ways.

It isn’t just about the strength and reason for correlation, we also shouldn’t limit ourselves to linear correlations. Non-linear correlations happen for various reasons, but a common one is diminishing returns. In most systems, having a little bit of something is a big deal, and every one after that matters a little less. In a messaging app, the first friend who texts you makes the app come alive. Each additional friend adds some pull, but your hundredth friend matters a lot less than your first or your tenth—you only have so much attention to give. Economists call this diminishing marginal utility: each new unit yields a smaller gain than the last. The same curve shows up in studying/exam results, income/happiness, marketing spend/impact, and many more such cases. It’s what gives a lot of empirical correlations a characteristic bend when viewed as a scatterplot.

Weak Strong

Lastly, and perhaps most tricky, life is littered with selection biases; what we observe is almost never perfectly representative of the overall population but is biased in one way or another. It is important for our simulated data to have similar selection biases. For example, a hospital in Canada noticed when analyzing bicycle accidents at the ER, wearing a helmet was correlated with having a concussion and you were ~50% more likely to have a serious injury compared to not wearing a helmet. That seems wrong, doesn’t it?

This is a specific form of selection bias called collider bias (or Berkson’s paradox). The hospital isn’t seeing all bike riders and all bike accidents; they don’t see all the cases where a bike rider is wearing a helmet and that helmet saved them from going to the ER. As a result, the helmet effectively filtered out lower-end accidents leaving only the more serious accidents for the ER.

You find this pattern all the time when doing data analysis. You see a study on what it takes to make a successful startup, but they only look at the ones who made it, not the ones that died out. You analyze active users and forget the ones who churned. The data you have is conditioned on having survived long enough to be recorded. It’s a kind of selection echo: the world you see isn’t the world as it is, but the world that lasted.

In the simulation below, I show how food quality and location can become inversely correlated, even if they start out completely independent. This happens because survival is a filter: a restaurant can survive with bad food if it has high foot traffic (a tourist trap), and it can survive in a bad location if the food is amazing. But if it has bad food and a bad location, it goes out of business and disappears from the dataset. We only see the survivors.

Combine this all together and you get data that is filled with correlations, large and small, inverse and positive, linear and not-so-linear, spurious and true. Or in other words, data that is actually worth analyzing.

Shape

I’ve long been fascinated by the beautifully smooth shapes that data makes when generated at scale. Not just systems, but data that is based on human behavior. I once assumed that because individual humans are so complicated, so individual, so hard to predict individually, that a bunch of humans would be exponentially more complicated to predict. But it is, in fact, the opposite. When you get lots of people, all the individual differences wash out, and what you are left with is the smooth underlying generative mechanisms that underlie their common behavior.

Most people are familiar with the bell curve or normal distribution. Plot human height and you’ll get something roughly normal. Human height follows this pattern because it’s the sum of many small, independent effects: genes, nutrition, environment. You can see below that adult human height is approximately normal; if you split by gender even more so.

Roll a bunch of dice, add them up, record that sum, repeat many times, and you’ll get the same shape; that’s the central limit theorem at work. When I see a bell-curve I see a process that has a bunch of uncorrelated randomness that is being added together. In the simulation below, try running it and seeing how as you add more samples it gets closer and closer to a smooth normal distribution.

Most of the data I’ve worked with doesn’t follow a normal distribution, though. Systems and behaviors rarely follow additive processes. They are more commonly multiplicative and/or full of feedback loops—both of which create long right tails.

For example, housing prices are generally right-skewed, largely because each property’s value grows through a chain of proportional effects: land value, size, location premiums, amenities, and market appreciation all compound on top of one another. Small percentage differences in these factors multiply rather than add. This makes the main body of the distribution log-normal; it is log simply because logarithms turns multiplication problems into addition problems. Remember, normal is additive, log-normal is multiplicative. For that reason, it is common to look at these right-skewed distributions in log space.

Below, home sales data from England and Wales is charted; try viewing in both linear and log space.

Source: HM Land Registry Price Paid Data, England & Wales (2024)

We can get something similar using our same dice rolling example. But this time, rather than adding the dice, we will multiply them together.

Many human systems aren’t just multiplicative—they’re self-reinforcing. Algorithms frequently elevate videos, products, games, or songs based on existing popularity, which in turn makes them even more popular. Because attention is finite, these dynamics often lead to winner-takes-most outcomes. This kind of feedback loop—known as preferential attachment—naturally produces highly right-skewed, power-law distributions.

When I first started plotting data—any kind of data—on user engagement, I was struck by how often these extreme right-skewed curves appeared. They looked like the chart below of reviews per game on Steam. Technically, both the reviews per game on Steam and the housing price data above are a mix of log-normal on the left, power-law on the right (I prefer to call it a mullet distribution). Multiplicative effects dominate in one regime, preferential attachment in another. The Steam data is just more dominated by power-law than housing prices are, likely because of the strength of the popularity dynamics I described above.

Steam reviews per game

You can make preferential attachment appear in a simulation by making prior success increase the odds of future success. In the simulation below I have an example of a distribution generated solely on preferential attachment.

Getting these shapes to emerge naturally is key. When I’m building simulations, I never directly sample these distributions. Instead, I code my agents so that, taken together, they arrive at those shapes honestly. I create the feedback loops that produce power-law distributions. I make processes multiplicative where they should be, and allow for multimodality by giving categories different generative properties.

Time

When I worked at Snap, I could tell when holidays were happening without ever doing something as prosaic as checking a calendar. I’d just look at time-series charts of user engagement, split by region. If people started taking pictures at six or seven in the morning, it was a work or school day. If usage didn’t spike until around 10 in the morning, it was a weekend or holiday.

Anyone who has looked at these time-series is familiar with their rhythms. For example, below is daily demand for electricity in California for the past three years. You can see the weekly peaks plus the greater demand for electricity in summer. Summer strikes again with its many correlations.

Real data shows this rhythm for several reasons:

  • You see it across a day because we sleep, work, and live as the earth spins and brings day and night.
  • You see it across a week based on however your culture defines weekends and weekdays; Friday nights out, Sunday nights in.
  • And you see it across a year, driven by that same sun: the seasons, and the layers we’ve added on top—holidays, festivals, school breaks, and all the rituals that divide our time into meaning.

In the visualization below, I multiply these temporal components—daily, weekly, and yearly—to approximate the kinds of cycles that appear in real time series. Conceptually, it’s similar to seasonal–trend decomposition, where a signal is separated into trend and seasonal components for analysis or forecasting. The difference is that here I’m composing those cycles from the ground up rather than decomposing observed data.

Weekly drag dots
Annual drag dots
Trend drag dots
Combined (3 years) driven by controls above

I combine those cycles with holidays—which turn weekdays into weekends—and make them an integral part of the causal DAG that drives my agents. By giving the root nodes those rhythms and letting them propagate through the graph, the model naturally produces the kinds of correlated effects that trip people up—spurious patterns like, “Hey, I think ice cream causes murder!”

Emergent Complexity

Now that we know what our data should look like, how do we achieve that without manually faking every data point? That sounds so complex!

It does. But we’re in luck; we don’t have to (and we shouldn’t) code the complexity directly. We rely on it emerging. When programming our simulations, we can focus on just the primary generative mechanisms (with some added individual-level truly random noise), and generate an overall more complex simulation with very simple individual-level rules.

The fact that complexity can arise from simple rules is well established. Boids is the classic example: three simple rules—steer away from crowds, move with the flock, and head toward its center of mass—produce beautiful flocking behavior. That’s always the goal: rich, organic behavior that feels real but emerges from simple, understandable rules. Try adjusting the relative strength of those three simple rules in the simulation below; you can see the mix of effects that emerge.

1.5
1.0
1.0

My agents are generally utility-driven; each agent has a utility function that it tries to maximize at every step. Individually, they’re single-minded and unintelligent, and if I relied on any one of them alone, the simulation would quickly collapse into some pathological or divergent behavior.

To avoid that, I build a range of intentionally simple strategies. One set of agents repeats whatever was most profitable in the past; another acts randomly; another imitates whatever has been most popular recently.

What I’ve discovered over years of building these systems is that when I combine many such agents—each using different but simple heuristics—the overall system becomes surprisingly robust and often appears intelligent. It’s a form of the wisdom of the crowds: a collection of uncorrelated, naïve guesses can, when aggregated, produce remarkably accurate behavior.

I create balance in the system without hard-coded limits by putting agents in tension with one another. As an example, I have a simple predator-prey simulation below: the prey eat grass, predators eat the prey. When there are too many prey, the grass thins and predators thrive; when there are too many predators, they starve. The system naturally ebbs and flows as everyone does their part to keep it in rhythmic balance. You can play around with the levers to see if you can make the system stay in balance without the ecosystem collapsing.

I usually introduce some form of survival of the fittest to stabilize things. I’m not afraid to let agents die if they can’t achieve their utility, but I’m always spawning new ones. When new agents appear, they mutate off the strategies of the successful ones. Winning strategies get copied (with variation), and the rest die off.

Over time, the system reaches a kind of equilibrium. I never expose day zero of my simulations; things are too weird then, too obviously hand-tuned. Instead, I let the world run for a while and settle; I let the genetic algorithms do their thing. I graph everything, check the curves, adjust the balance. For many processes, I already have strong expectations on what everything should look like, because I’ve seen the equivalent in my work many times over. When I haven’t, I search through papers and find empirical observations I can ensure my simulation matches the same generative spirit.

It is less pure engineering and more gardening. I tend to my simulation as much as I build it. Little worlds, carefully grown, for students to explore.
